History and Physical (H&P – Detailed)

Consult Summary:
32-year-old married man with known hypothyroidism presents with 2 months of worsening fatigue, poor sleep, low mood, decreased appetite, reduced libido, and exertional shortness of breath that began after starting a new job.

History:
• Presenting complaint – “no energy,” difficulty getting up, and daytime tiredness for ≈2 months.  
• Timeline – Symptoms started shortly after beginning a new job (~2 months ago) and have persisted/worsened.  
• Sleep – Difficulty sleeping; not waking early but struggles to fall or stay asleep.  
• Appetite – Eating less than usual.  
• Concentration – Easily distracted, hard to focus.  
• Mood – Feels “lower” than usual; not clearly happy or unhappy; wants to return to prior baseline.  
• Libido – Decreased interest in sex over the same period; no perceived change in morning erections.  
• Dyspnea – Noticeable shortness of breath during sports/exercise compared with a few months ago.  
• Suicidality – Denies thoughts of self-harm or harming others.  
• Vision – No changes.  
• Review of systems – No other specific positives or negatives elicited.

Past Medical History:
• Hypothyroidism – On chronic thyroxine replacement; details of dosing, monitoring, and last thyroid function tests not discussed.  
• No prior psychiatric diagnoses reported.  
• No other chronic medical conditions noted.

Medications:
• Thyroxine (levothyroxine) – dose/route/frequency not documented.  
Allergies:
• Denies medication allergies.

Social History:
• Married; no children mentioned.  
• Started a new job 2 months ago.  
• Participates in sports.  
• Tobacco, alcohol, and recreational drug use not discussed.

Family History:
• Father died by suicide 15 years ago.  
• Mother alive and well.  
• No known family history of depression or other major illnesses besides the above.

Physical Examination:
• Vitals: Not recorded.  
• General / HEENT / CV / Resp / Abd / Neuro / Psych: Not performed (tele-consult).

Investigations:
• None to date.  
• Plan to arrange blood tests (including thyroid function and basic screen) and in-person examination with GP.

Assessment & Plan:
Overall Impression:
Multifactorial fatigue with low mood and exertional dyspnea. Leading considerations are major depressive disorder versus under-treated hypothyroidism; anemia and other metabolic causes also possible.

DDx Integration (brief):
1. Major depressive disorder – Supports: low mood, insomnia, anhedonia (libido ↓), appetite ↓, fatigue, poor concentration; temporal link to work stress. Opposes: patient emphasizes energy more than sadness; no suicidality.  
2. Sub-optimally treated hypothyroidism – Supports: known diagnosis, fatigue, low mood, libido ↓, exertional SOB. Opposes: no classic weight gain/cold intolerance; no recent medication change documented.  
3. Anemia – Supports: fatigue, exertional SOB, reduced intake. Opposes: no bleeding history or pallor reported.

Issue 1 – Fatigue/Low Mood:
• Assessment: 2-month history consistent with possible depression or endocrine/metabolic cause.  
• Plan:
  – Arrange GP appointment within a few days for full physical exam.  
  – Order labs: CBC, TSH/free T4, electrolytes, renal/liver profile, ferritin, vitamin B12/folate, fasting glucose.  
  – Screen formally for depression (e.g., PHQ-9) at in-person visit.  
  – Provide brief supportive counseling; advised patient of red-flag symptoms (worsening mood, suicidality) and to seek help urgently if they arise.  
  – Consider referral to mental-health services depending on results.

Issue 2 – Known Hypothyroidism:
• Assessment: Possible inadequate replacement.  
• Plan:
  – Check adherence and current levothyroxine dose.  
  – Repeat thyroid function tests with above labs.  
  – Adjust dose per results and clinical response.

Issue 3 – Exertional Shortness of Breath:
• Assessment: Could be deconditioning, anemia, thyroid-related myopathy, or cardiorespiratory issue.  
• Plan:
  – Evaluate with physical exam (heart, lungs) during GP visit.  
  – Include CBC and consider chest auscultation; further tests (CXR, ECG) only if indicated by findings.

General plan items:
• Follow-up: GP to review exam and lab results; schedule virtual follow-up if symptoms persist or lab abnormalities found.  
• Safety-netting: Patient advised to seek immediate care if severe SOB, chest pain, or suicidal thoughts develop.

Quality checks:
● Missing elements: No vitals, physical exam, or recent thyroid/lab data recorded; substance use history not obtained; medication dose unspecified; allergies documented.  
● No transcript/DDx conflicts noted (minor clarification on morning erections acknowledged).  
● Transcript quality: Clear audio; minor freezing but information adequate.
